**Yes.** The ending grows out of what the story sets up early on. Barbara's belief that "history felt suspended" and that "nothing bad could penetrate walls this expensive" is the illusion the climax shatters. Her realization that they "had not escaped history after all" but "merely brought it with them" closes that thematic arc directly.

The baby's final kick echoes the earlier "slow, rolling turn" and her worries about the world the child would enter, so the closing image feels deliberate rather than tacked on. The coda in the parking lot also gives the chaos a moment to settle. The brief flash-forward to the Rabbi's death resolves the central event. The ending lands as the moment the piece has been building toward, not an arbitrary stopping point.
